summary:
Errante is a public web tool that lets anyone watch how a patch of sky changes over time in images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users choose an object or enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec), and Errante shows the series of observations as a blinking sequence, making moving and variable objects easy to spot.

Our pipeline retrieves SPHEREx image cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, removes zodiacal light, masks bad pixels, groups exposures into epochs, and reprojects them onto a common grid so fixed stars stay in place. The viewer offers epoch-by-epoch blinking with date and wavelength, difference images, a co-moving stack that follows the target, zoom and pan, and URL parameters for sharing and embedding. It is built to be refreshed easily as new SPHEREx data arrive.

We tested it with real data on WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Moving-object searches have led to discoveries since Pluto, and SPHEREx produces more data than any one person can review. Errante makes that search accessible to everyone.
details:
What it does
Errante is a web tool that shows how a small patch of sky changes over time in images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. You pick an object (or enter RA/Dec coordinates) and a detector, and the viewer plays the observations like a short movie. Stars stay fixed, while anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. We were inspired by how Pluto was found by comparing two images of the sky, and we wanted to give that same experience to anyone, not only to astronomers.

How it works
SPHEREx observes with filters that change across the detector, so each exposure captures a different wavelength. That means we can’t just flip through raw images. Our Python pipeline first searches NASA/IPAC IRSA for images covering the target and keeps a local index, so IRSA is only queried once. It then downloads small cutouts, subtracts zodiacal light, and masks bad pixels. Next, it groups exposures into epochs, stacks them, and reprojects everything onto a common grid (north up, east left) so fixed stars land on the same pixels. It also computes where the target should be at each epoch from its proper motion. Finally, it renders frames with one fixed brightness scale, so changes between frames are real and not display effects. The output is PNG files plus a JSON manifest that a static web viewer reads.

What users can do
Blink between epochs with play, pause and a slider, with the date and wavelength shown for each frame. They can switch to a difference view (epoch minus median of all epochs) to highlight movers, or a co-moving stack that follows the object to boost its signal. They can zoom, pan, show or hide the expected-position marker, and open any view with URL parameters, which makes it easy to share or embed.

Tools
Python 3.13, Astropy, reproject, astroquery, NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib for processing; HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas) for the viewer; and Vercel for hosting. Data: SPHEREx images from NASA/JPL-Caltech via IRSA.

What we considered
We designed it so new SPHEREx releases can be added by rerunning the pipeline with a refresh option. We also chose a static viewer so it is simple to host and fast to load. We tested with real data on WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. IRSA was sometimes unavailable, so we added retries and a local index.

Limitations and next steps
We have not yet visually confirmed WISE 0855 in the images, so the red marker shows where it should be but is not a detection. Epsilon Indi B is still pending because name resolution failed, and some detectors have too few epochs. Next, we want Gaia and WISE overlays, per-band spectra, and a selectable field of view.

AI use
We used AI tools (Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT) to speed up coding, testing and documentation. We chose the idea, scope and design decisions, and we ran and checked the results ourselves. All images in the project are real SPHEREx data processed by code, not AI-generated.
Repository

https://github.com/JaimeGD07/Errante
